newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ dollar ends stronger as U.S. dollar falls.
newsitem.headline: NZ dollar ends stronger as U.S. dollar falls.

text.p: The New Zealand dollar closed stronger on Wednesday in response to a fall in the U.S. dollar after a report showing surprising strength in Japan's economy.
Dealers said shorts clawed back as the greenback slumped and further shorts are set just above the closing level of US$0.6857/64.
The kiwi opened at 0.6846/53. The Trade-Weighted Index ended slightly firmer at 67.19 from its 67.10 opening.
Dealers said the Tankan survey of Japanese sentiment showed a much stronger than expected economy which suggests Japan may have to raise rates sooner than picked.

That is likely to see pressure developing on the New Zealand Trade-Weighted Index and with the Monetary Conditions Index already seen beyond the Reserve Bank's perceived tolerance level, dealers predict the Kiwi's downside may be limited.
How far the U.S. dollar is allowed to sink against the yen will also be uppermost in local traders' minds.
"How the Reserve Bank reacts on Friday to a weak U.S. dollar will also be an interesting question," said one dealer.
The RB releases its Monetary Policy Statement on Friday and dealers expect the bank to endorse a 75 basis point easing over the March level it set.
However, with the MCI already 112 basis points below the March level, the market's attention will centre on how much the bank will allow rates to move outside its desired level.
"With the MCI down here there's limited ability to see it lower even though it has been as low as 125," said one dealer.
Preceeding the MPS is Treasuer Winston Peters' first budget, but dealers doubt it will have much effect on the currency.
"I don't think the dollar will be influenced by the budget because we have had all the bad news," said one.

The RB is predicted to allow a further easing later in the year as long as markets do not pre-empt that. And that is expected to give the Kiwi an overall weakening bias. But an immediate fall from here is seen as premature, dealers said.
